Living organisms.intro: This topic covers the foundation of Biology: what makes something living, the cell as the basic unit of life, the major structures and functions of plant and animal cells, and the levels at which living things are organized. These are high-value UTME areas because questions often test definitions, comparisons, functions, examples and the correct sequence of biological organization.

blocks.x: 1. What is a living organism?

A **living organism** is an individual living thing that carries out the activities necessary for life. Examples include humans, other animals, green plants, fungi, bacteria and many single-celled organisms such as Amoeba and Paramecium.

The important idea is that life is identified by a **combination of life processes**, not by one feature alone. For example, a fire can move and grow, but it is not a living organism because it does not possess the complete organization and biological processes of life.
For UTME, do not memorize only the names of the characteristics. Understand what each characteristic means and be able to recognize an example of it.
2. Characteristics of living organisms

The major characteristics commonly used to recognize living organisms are **Movement, Respiration, Nutrition, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction and Excretion**. Homeostasis is also an important property of living organisms because living systems regulate their internal conditions.

head: Characteristic
What it means
Example
rows: Change in position of the whole organism or part of it
Amoeba changes position; a plant shoot bends toward light
Release of usable energy from food
Glucose is broken down to release energy
Green plants photosynthesize; humans eat food
Ability to detect and respond to stimuli
Permanent increase in size and/or dry mass due to increase in cell number/size

blocks.x: 2.1 Movement

Movement is a change in position of the whole organism or of one of its parts. Animals usually show obvious movement because they can move from one place to another. Plants are also living and show movement, although it is often slow and occurs through growth responses or movement of plant parts.

Examples include the movement of Amoeba by pseudopodia, movement of cilia in Paramecium, and the bending of a shoot toward light. A plant does not have to walk from one place to another before it can be said to move.

blocks.x: 2.2 Respiration

Respiration is the controlled chemical process by which cells release usable energy from food. The energy released is used for activities such as movement, growth, active transport, repair and reproduction.

**Aerobic respiration** uses oxygen and generally releases more energy. A simplified word equation is: **glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy**. Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen and releases less energy.
Respiration is not the same as breathing. **Breathing** is the physical movement of air into and out of respiratory organs, while **respiration** is a chemical process occurring in cells.
2.3 Nutrition
Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain and use nutrients needed for energy, growth, repair and maintenance.

Green plants are mainly **autotrophic** because they manufacture organic food from inorganic raw materials by photosynthesis. Animals and fungi are generally **heterotrophic** because they obtain organic nutrients from other organisms or organic matter.

Photosynthesis can be summarized as: **carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen**, in the presence of light and chlorophyll. The glucose may be converted to other substances such as starch for storage.
2.4 Sensitivity / irritability

Sensitivity is the ability of an organism to detect changes in its internal or external environment and respond to them. A change that causes a response is called a **stimulus**; the response is the reaction to that stimulus.
Examples include withdrawal of the hand from a hot object, closing of the eyes in very bright light, and growth of a plant shoot toward light.
2.5 Growth
Growth is a permanent and usually irreversible increase in size, mass and/or dry mass of an organism or its parts. In multicellular organisms, growth commonly involves cell division and enlargement.

A key biological distinction is that true growth is not simply temporary swelling caused by taking in water. In many organisms, growth involves an increase in cellular material and therefore a lasting increase in living structure.
2.6 Reproduction
Reproduction is the process by which organisms produce new individuals of their own kind. It ensures **continuity of life** from one generation to another.

In **asexual reproduction**, one parent is involved and offspring are usually genetically very similar to the parent. In **sexual reproduction**, genetic material from two gametes combines, producing variation among offspring.
2.7 Excretion
Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste products produced inside the body. Common metabolic wastes include carbon dioxide, excess water and nitrogenous wastes such as urea in humans.
Excretion must not be confused with egestion. **Egestion** is the removal of undigested food from the digestive tract; **excretion** removes substances produced by metabolism.
2.8 Homeostasis

Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions so that they remain within suitable limits despite changes in the external environment. Examples include regulation of body temperature, blood glucose concentration and water balance.
3. The cell: basic unit of life

The **cell** is the basic structural and functional unit of life. Structural means that organisms are built from cells; functional means that essential life activities are carried out by cells or by groups of cells.
Some organisms, such as Amoeba, consist of a single cell and are therefore **unicellular**. Others, such as humans and maize plants, contain many specialized cells and are **multicellular**.
A unicellular organism performs all necessary life processes within one cell. A multicellular organism divides work among specialized cells, tissues and organs.
4. Basic cell organization

A typical cell contains a **cell membrane**, **cytoplasm** and, in eukaryotic cells, a **nucleus**. Plant cells also have a **cell wall**, **chloroplasts** in photosynthetic tissues and a large **vacuole** containing cell sap.

head: Cell component
Main function
Important point
rows: Controls movement of substances into and out of the cell
Contains genetic material and controls many cell activities
Site of aerobic respiration and major ATP production
Cells with high energy demand often have many

blocks.x: 5.1 Cell membrane
The cell membrane forms the boundary between the cell and its surroundings. It is **selectively permeable**, meaning that its structure allows some substances to cross more easily than others.

The membrane helps the cell maintain suitable internal conditions. Substances may cross by diffusion, osmosis or active transport, depending on the substance and concentration/water potential conditions.
5.2 Cytoplasm

The cytoplasm is the living material inside the cell membrane, excluding the nucleus in a typical eukaryotic cell description. It contains the organelles and is the site of many chemical reactions involved in metabolism.
5.3 Nucleus

The nucleus contains genetic material in the form of chromosomes and helps regulate cell activities by controlling gene expression. During cell division, chromosomes are copied and distributed to daughter cells.
5.4 Mitochondria
Mitochondria are major sites of aerobic respiration. They contain enzymes involved in energy-releasing pathways and produce ATP, which is a readily usable form of cellular energy.
Cells that require large amounts of energy often contain numerous mitochondria. Examples include muscle cells, which need energy for contraction.
5.5 Ribosomes
Ribosomes are the structures where amino acids are assembled into proteins. Therefore, whenever a question asks for the site of **protein synthesis**, think **ribosome**.
5.6 Cell wall

The plant cell wall is a rigid layer outside the cell membrane. It provides mechanical support, helps maintain cell shape and prevents the cell from bursting when water enters under suitable conditions.
5.7 Chloroplast
Chloroplasts are found in photosynthetic plant cells and contain chlorophyll. They are the organelles where photosynthesis occurs. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy used to drive photosynthesis.
5.8 Vacuole

A mature plant cell commonly contains a large permanent vacuole surrounded by the tonoplast and filled with cell sap. The vacuole helps maintain **turgor pressure**, which contributes to support in non-woody plant tissues.
6. Plant cell versus animal cell

head: Feature
Plant cell
Animal cell
rows: Usually absent or small temporary vacuoles
Generally absent in higher plant cells

blocks.x: 7. Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
Cells can also be grouped by internal organization. **Prokaryotic cells** do not have a membrane-bound nucleus. Their genetic material lies in a nucleoid region. Bacteria are the main examples.
**Eukaryotic cells** have a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Animals, plants, fungi and protists are eukaryotic.

head: Feature
Prokaryotic cell
Eukaryotic cell
rows: Usually circular DNA in nucleoid; may also have plasmids

blocks.x: Do not say that prokaryotes have no DNA. They have DNA; the important difference is that it is not enclosed inside a membrane-bound nucleus.
8. Levels of organization in living organisms

Multicellular organisms are organized from simpler units into larger functional levels. For the sequence emphasized in the JAMB Biology syllabus, remember: **cell → tissue → organ → system → organism**.

head: Level
Meaning
Example
rows: Group of similar cells performing a common function
Organs working together for a major function

blocks.cap: Increasing organizational complexity in a multicellular organism.

blocks.x: 9. Understanding each level

A **cell** is a single basic unit. When similar cells are organized to perform a particular function, they form a **tissue**. Different tissues combine to form an **organ**. Several organs work together as an **organ system**, and all the systems together make the complete **organism**.

For example, in a human: muscle cells contribute to muscle tissue; different tissues form the heart; the heart works with blood vessels and other organs in the circulatory system; the circulatory system is part of the complete human organism.
10. Specialized cells
In multicellular organisms, cells become specialized for particular functions. Specialization means that a cell develops structural features that make it well suited to a particular job.

head: Specialized cell
Adaptation / feature
Function
rows: Biconcave shape; no nucleus at maturity in mammals; haemoglobin
Move mucus or other material along a surface

blocks.x: 11. Why cell specialization matters

Specialization creates a **division of labour**. Instead of every cell performing every task equally, different cells become efficient at particular functions. This makes complex multicellular organisms possible.
12. Important distinctions UTME can test

head: Do not confuse
Correct distinction
rows: Respiration is cellular energy release; breathing is movement of air in and out of respiratory surfaces.
Excretion removes metabolic waste; egestion removes undigested food.
Growth is permanent increase in size/mass; movement is change in position of an organism or part.
Nutrition is obtaining/using nutrients; digestion breaks large insoluble food molecules into smaller soluble molecules.
Cell wall gives support and is not selectively permeable like the cell membrane; cell membrane controls exchange.
Tissue is a group of similar cells with a common function; an organ contains different tissues working together.

blocks.x: 13. Worked application examples

blocks.q: A student says, 'Plants are not living because they do not move from one place to another.' Is the statement correct? Explain.
steps: The statement is incorrect because movement does not require the whole organism to travel from one location to another.
Plants show movement through changes in the position of parts, such as shoots bending toward light and roots growing in response to stimuli.
Therefore, lack of locomotion does not mean that a plant is non-living.
blocks.ans: Plants are living. They show movement of their parts and also carry out respiration, nutrition, growth, sensitivity, reproduction and excretion.

blocks.q: A cell contains a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole. What type of cell is it most likely to be?
steps: A cell wall is a major supporting feature of plant cells.
Chloroplasts indicate photosynthetic plant tissue.
A large permanent vacuole is also characteristic of mature plant cells.
Therefore, the combination strongly identifies a plant cell.
blocks.ans: A typical mature photosynthetic plant cell.

blocks.q: Arrange these in increasing level of organization: organ, organism, tissue, cell, system.
steps: Start with the smallest basic living unit: cell.
Cells form tissues.
Tissues combine to form organs.
Organs work together in systems.
All systems together make the complete organism.

blocks.q: Which structure would you expect to be especially numerous in a muscle cell that is highly active?
steps: Muscle contraction requires a large supply of usable energy.
Aerobic respiration occurs mainly in mitochondria.
Therefore, a highly active muscle cell is expected to contain many mitochondria.

blocks.q: A substance is produced as a waste product of metabolism and must be removed from the body. Is this excretion or egestion?
steps: The key phrase is 'produced by metabolism'.
Excretion deals with metabolic waste products such as carbon dioxide and urea.
Egestion deals with undigested food remaining in the digestive tract.

blocks.x: 14. Exam-ready summary

items: Living organisms carry out a combination of life processes; no single characteristic should be used alone to define life.
Movement may involve the whole organism or only part of it; plants can therefore show movement.
Respiration is a chemical energy-releasing process and is different from breathing.
Nutrition supplies materials needed for energy, growth, repair and maintenance.
Sensitivity is the ability to detect and respond to stimuli.
Growth is a permanent increase in size, mass and/or dry mass.
Reproduction produces new individuals and ensures continuity of life.
Excretion removes metabolic wastes; egestion removes undigested food.
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
Cell membrane controls exchange; cytoplasm is the site of many reactions; nucleus contains genetic material and helps control activities.
Mitochondria are major sites of aerobic respiration; ribosomes are sites of protein synthesis.
Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts in photosynthetic cells and a large permanent vacuole.
Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotic cells possess one.
The main sequence of multicellular organization is cell → tissue → organ → system → organism.

blocks.x: 15. Final self-check questions

Before starting Topic Practice, make sure you can answer these without looking back: (1) What are the major characteristics of living organisms? (2) Why is respiration different from breathing? (3) What is the function of the cell membrane? (4) What is the site of protein synthesis? (5) Give three differences between plant and animal cells. (6) What is the difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells? (7) Arrange cell, tissue, organ, system and organism in the correct order. (8) Why does a muscle cell contain many mitochondria? (9) Distinguish excretion from egestion. (10) Why is the cell described as the basic unit of life?

The membrane helps the cell maintain suitable internal conditions. Substances may cross by diffusion, osmosis or active transport, depending on the substance and concentration/water potential conditions.
5.2 Cytoplasm

The cytoplasm is the living material inside the cell membrane, excluding the nucleus in a typical eukaryotic cell description. It contains the organelles and is the site of many chemical reactions involved in metabolism.
5.3 Nucleus

The nucleus contains genetic material in the form of chromosomes and helps regulate cell activities by controlling gene expression. During cell division, chromosomes are copied and distributed to daughter cells.
5.4 Mitochondria
Mitochondria are major sites of aerobic respiration. They contain enzymes involved in energy-releasing pathways and produce ATP, which is a readily usable form of cellular energy.
Cells that require large amounts of energy often contain numerous mitochondria. Examples include muscle cells, which need energy for contraction.
5.5 Ribosomes
Ribosomes are the structures where amino acids are assembled into proteins. Therefore, whenever a question asks for the site of **protein synthesis**, think **ribosome**.
5.6 Cell wall

The plant cell wall is a rigid layer outside the cell membrane. It provides mechanical support, helps maintain cell shape and prevents the cell from bursting when water enters under suitable conditions.
5.7 Chloroplast
Chloroplasts are found in photosynthetic plant cells and contain chlorophyll. They are the organelles where photosynthesis occurs. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy used to drive photosynthesis.
5.8 Vacuole

A mature plant cell commonly contains a large permanent vacuole surrounded by the tonoplast and filled with cell sap. The vacuole helps maintain **turgor pressure**, which contributes to support in non-woody plant tissues.
6. Plant cell versus animal cell

head: Feature
Plant cell
Animal cell
rows: Usually absent or small temporary vacuoles
Generally absent in higher plant cells

blocks.cap: The two cell types share many structures, but plant cells have several features associated with photosynthesis and rigidity.

blocks.x: 7. Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
Cells can also be grouped by internal organization. **Prokaryotic cells** do not have a membrane-bound nucleus. Their genetic material lies in a nucleoid region. Bacteria are the main examples.
**Eukaryotic cells** have a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Animals, plants, fungi and protists are eukaryotic.

head: Feature
Prokaryotic cell
Eukaryotic cell
rows: Usually circular DNA in nucleoid; may also have plasmids

blocks.x: Do not say that prokaryotes have no DNA. They have DNA; the important difference is that it is not enclosed inside a membrane-bound nucleus.
8. Levels of organization in living organisms

Multicellular organisms are organized from simpler units into larger functional levels. For the sequence emphasized in the JAMB Biology syllabus, remember: **cell → tissue → organ → system → organism**.

head: Level
Meaning
Example
rows: Group of similar cells performing a common function
Organs working together for a major function

blocks.cap: Increasing organizational complexity in a multicellular organism.

blocks.x: 9. Understanding each level

A **cell** is a single basic unit. When similar cells are organized to perform a particular function, they form a **tissue**. Different tissues combine to form an **organ**. Several organs work together as an **organ system**, and all the systems together make the complete **organism**.

For example, in a human: muscle cells contribute to muscle tissue; different tissues form the heart; the heart works with blood vessels and other organs in the circulatory system; the circulatory system is part of the complete human organism.
10. Specialized cells
In multicellular organisms, cells become specialized for particular functions. Specialization means that a cell develops structural features that make it well suited to a particular job.

head: Specialized cell
Adaptation / feature
Function
rows: Biconcave shape; no nucleus at maturity in mammals; haemoglobin
Move mucus or other material along a surface

blocks.x: 11. Why cell specialization matters

Specialization creates a **division of labour**. Instead of every cell performing every task equally, different cells become efficient at particular functions. This makes complex multicellular organisms possible.
12. Important distinctions UTME can test

head: Do not confuse
Correct distinction
rows: Respiration is cellular energy release; breathing is movement of air in and out of respiratory surfaces.
Excretion removes metabolic waste; egestion removes undigested food.
Growth is permanent increase in size/mass; movement is change in position of an organism or part.
Nutrition is obtaining/using nutrients; digestion breaks large insoluble food molecules into smaller soluble molecules.
Cell wall gives support and is not selectively permeable like the cell membrane; cell membrane controls exchange.
Tissue is a group of similar cells with a common function; an organ contains different tissues working together.

blocks.x: 13. Worked application examples

blocks.q: A student says, 'Plants are not living because they do not move from one place to another.' Is the statement correct? Explain.
steps: The statement is incorrect because movement does not require the whole organism to travel from one location to another.
Plants show movement through changes in the position of parts, such as shoots bending toward light and roots growing in response to stimuli.
Therefore, lack of locomotion does not mean that a plant is non-living.
blocks.ans: Plants are living. They show movement of their parts and also carry out respiration, nutrition, growth, sensitivity, reproduction and excretion.

blocks.q: A cell contains a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole. What type of cell is it most likely to be?
steps: A cell wall is a major supporting feature of plant cells.
Chloroplasts indicate photosynthetic plant tissue.
A large permanent vacuole is also characteristic of mature plant cells.
Therefore, the combination strongly identifies a plant cell.
blocks.ans: A typical mature photosynthetic plant cell.

blocks.q: Arrange these in increasing level of organization: organ, organism, tissue, cell, system.
steps: Start with the smallest basic living unit: cell.
Cells form tissues.
Tissues combine to form organs.
Organs work together in systems.
All systems together make the complete organism.

blocks.q: Which structure would you expect to be especially numerous in a muscle cell that is highly active?
steps: Muscle contraction requires a large supply of usable energy.
Aerobic respiration occurs mainly in mitochondria.
Therefore, a highly active muscle cell is expected to contain many mitochondria.

blocks.q: A substance is produced as a waste product of metabolism and must be removed from the body. Is this excretion or egestion?
steps: The key phrase is 'produced by metabolism'.
Excretion deals with metabolic waste products such as carbon dioxide and urea.
Egestion deals with undigested food remaining in the digestive tract.

blocks.x: 14. Exam-ready summary

items: Living organisms carry out a combination of life processes; no single characteristic should be used alone to define life.
Movement may involve the whole organism or only part of it; plants can therefore show movement.
Respiration is a chemical energy-releasing process and is different from breathing.
Nutrition supplies materials needed for energy, growth, repair and maintenance.
Sensitivity is the ability to detect and respond to stimuli.
Growth is a permanent increase in size, mass and/or dry mass.
Reproduction produces new individuals and ensures continuity of life.
Excretion removes metabolic wastes; egestion removes undigested food.
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
Cell membrane controls exchange; cytoplasm is the site of many reactions; nucleus contains genetic material and helps control activities.
Mitochondria are major sites of aerobic respiration; ribosomes are sites of protein synthesis.
Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts in photosynthetic cells and a large permanent vacuole.
Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotic cells possess one.
The main sequence of multicellular organization is cell → tissue → organ → system → organism.

blocks.x: 15. Final self-check questions

Before starting Topic Practice, make sure you can answer these without looking back: (1) What are the major characteristics of living organisms? (2) Why is respiration different from breathing? (3) What is the function of the cell membrane? (4) What is the site of protein synthesis? (5) Give three differences between plant and animal cells. (6) What is the difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells? (7) Arrange cell, tissue, organ, system and organism in the correct order. (8) Why does a muscle cell contain many mitochondria? (9) Distinguish excretion from egestion. (10) Why is the cell described as the basic unit of life?
